title: Thai floods expose waste pollution in 'garbage dump' region
summary: Father of four Adisorn Lakonburee used to catch fish for his family's dinner, but stopped after floodwaters brought oil slicks and foul chemical smells into his village in eastern Thailand.

Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked reputable news agency proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources Located between the capital Bangkok and Thailand's flagship industrial zone farther east, Prachinburi has long had a problem with pollution. Father of four Adisorn Lakonburee used to catch fish for his family's dinner, but stopped after floodwaters brought oil slicks and foul chemical smells into his village in eastern Thailand. "Now I'm too afraid to catch or eat them," the 43-year-old homebuilder told AFP at his home in Prachinburi province, adding that he and his family are also too scared to drink the tap water. Located between the capital Bangkok and Thailand's flagship industrial zone farther east, Prachinburi has long faced concerns over waste pollution. But heavy flooding in September and October exposed the scale of the problem, spreading foul, rainbow-colored water across rice paddies and waterways. In water sampled near one landfill in October, Thai authorities found "unusually high" levels of petroleum hydrocarbons—chemicals associated with oil and fuel—as well as toxic concentrations of aluminum. The landfill operator, Green Environment Technology, denied any wrongdoing, but after resident complaints, the industry ministry ordered it temporarily closed. Foul, rainbow-colored water spread across rice paddies and waterways after heavy flooding in September and October. The ministry also suspended operations at two other waste facilities in the surrounding area and ordered a nationwide inspection of 3,000 similar plants across Thailand—with 300 already found to have breached regulations. As residents protested against the pollution, Prachinburi's then-acting governor ate locally caught fish to show residents it was safe. But Navaporn Sanguanmoo, director of industrial waste management in the government's Department of Industrial Works, said authorities needed to do more. "Prachinburi is a lesson that makes us rethink many things," she told AFP. Garbage dump Farmland stretches as far as the eye can see in Prachinburi, a major food-producing province known for rice, sugarcane, cassava and fruit orchards, as well as livestock and fish farming. But among the fields are waste facilities and illegal dumping sites. During a visit this month, AFP saw a pile of electronic scrap mixed with chicken manure in the middle of a sugarcane plantation, and a massive landfill hidden inside a forest. Prachinburi has been a "garbage dump" for Thailand's flagship industrial zone. A burning stench hung in the air near some of the sites, akin to machine oil or weed killer. Environmental researcher Somnuck Jongmeewasin said the area had been a "garbage dump" for the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC), a flagship industrial zone spanning the neighboring provinces of Rayong, Chonburi and Chachoengsao. An adviser to the Thai parliament's industrial subcommittee, he has conducted research that identified more than 60 suspected illegal dumping sites in Prachinburi in recent years. Dawan Chantarahassadee, an activist with environmental watchdog EARTH Thailand, blamed cheap land and lax law enforcement for what she described as an "empire" of waste facilities. The floods have "clearly shown that government oversight has not been strict enough," she said. Campaigners trace the problem to a 2016 military junta order that exempted waste facilities from town-planning laws, allowing them into agricultural green zones. "This area is designated for agriculture," said local activist Sumet Rianpongnam, 54. Prachinburi activists and residents hold a sign reading 'Prachinburi needs a pollution control zone' during a demonstration against waste pollution. "Yet (waste-processing) factories have been built right next to our homes." Last year, Thailand banned the import of plastic waste and strengthened controls on electronic waste to help protect the environment and public health. But Navaporn, from the industrial works department, said the country still deals with around 3 million metric tons (3.3 million tons) of hazardous industrial waste each year, and over 30 million metric tons (33 million tons) of nonhazardous waste. She said some can be sold, including scrap metal, but waste with little resale value, such as oil-contaminated water or low-grade plastics, was particularly vulnerable to illegal dumping because of high treatment costs. "That is precisely the type of waste we find illegally dumped across multiple areas," Navaporn said. She added that the penalties for dumping were too low, meaning "breaking the law makes economic sense" for violators. Waste facilities and illegal dumping sites are found across Prachinburi. At a Buddhist meditation center near a suspected dumping site, nun Suparpron Tapowpong, 64, said they have had to wash with rainwater and drink donated bottled water. "We just don't know where to get safe water anymore," she said, adding that "this has become a serious crisis, the worst I've ever faced."
